solution.concept_anchor: Antecedent drainage rivers predating Himalayan uplift
solution.strong_distractor: b — Sutlej is a strong distractor because it is a Punjab river (associated with the plains) and students who are uncertain about its antecedent nature may mark it as the odd one out, not realising it also originates in Tibet and cuts transversely through ranges.
elimination_logic: Antecedent rivers are those that predate the Himalayan uplift and cut through the rising mountains — Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra are the primary examples.
Sutlej also originates in Tibet (near Mansarovar at Rakshastal Lake) and cuts transversely through ranges — it is antecedent.
Chambal originates in the Vindhya Range (MP) — a Peninsular river, a consequent river following the post-uplift slope; it has nothing to do with Himalayan antecedent drainage.
Chambal is the odd one out among antecedent Himalayan rivers — select option d.
solution.final_explanation:
Antecedent drainage describes rivers that existed before the mountains they now cut through — their channels predate and override the uplift.

• Option (a) Indus: Antecedent — originates in Tibet, predates Himalayan uplift, cuts the western syntaxial bend at Nanga Parbat. Belongs to the group.
• Option (b) Sutlej: Antecedent — originates near Rakshastal Lake (Tibet), cuts through the Himalayas via Shipki La, enters Punjab. Belongs to the group.
• Option (c) Brahmaputra: Antecedent — longest antecedent river, originates in Tibet as Tsangpo, cuts eastern syntaxial bend at Namcha Barwa. Belongs to the group.
• Option (d) Chambal: ODD ONE OUT — a Peninsular river originating in the Vindhyas (Mhow, MP). It is a consequent river following the post-tectonic Peninsular slope. It has no antecedent relationship with any mountain-building episode.

Value Addition:
• Satluj (Sutlej) enters India through Shipki La in Himachal Pradesh — a documented entry point for map questions.
• The antecedent rivers' gorges are deeper than any valleys carved by normal erosion — the Indus gorge depth exceeds 5,000m in some sections.
• Ganga is not antecedent in the strictest sense — its current main channel post-dates Himalayan uplift; only its headwater tributaries show antecedent characteristics.

solution.concept_anchor: Sambhar largest inland salt lake Aravallis drainage Luni

statement_analysis.statement: Sambhar Salt Lake in Rajasthan is the largest inland salt lake in India and is of tectonic origin.
statement_analysis.reason: Sambhar is a tectonic basin in the Aravalli region — the largest inland saline water body in India, covering approximately 230 sq km (expanding during monsoon).

statement_analysis.statement: The Luni River, originating near Pushkar in the Aravalli foothills, ultimately drains into the Arabian Sea via the Rann of Kutch.
statement_analysis.reason: Luni drains INTO the Rann of Kutch — the Rann is a tidal salt marsh, not an outlet to the Arabian Sea in the conventional sense; the river terminates in the Rann and does not reach the open Arabian Sea as a flowing river.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) attracts students who know Luni ends in the Rann of Kutch area and imprecisely think 'Rann of Kutch = near Arabian Sea = Arabian Sea' without recognising the hydrological distinction between a terminal marsh and an ocean outlet.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Sambhar as largest inland salt lake of tectonic origin in Rajasthan — a precisely documented fact; mark Correct.

Statement 2: 'Drains into the Arabian Sea via the Rann of Kutch' — the Rann of Kutch is not a conduit to the Arabian Sea for Luni; the river terminates in the Rann, which is a terminal basin; mark Incorrect.
Statement 1 is correct, Statement 2 is incorrect — select option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 'via the Rann of Kutch' phrasing in Statement 2 is a scope-extension trap. Students who know 'Luni flows into the Rann of Kutch' may accept the addition 'and thereby into the Arabian Sea' as a reasonable geographic inference — after all, the Rann is connected to the Gulf of Kutch during high tides. But as a riverine drainage endpoint, Luni terminates in the Rann; it does not have a defined channel outlet to the Arabian Sea.
solution.final_explanation:
The Luni and Sambhar are the two most important endorheic/saline water body features of the Thar Desert drainage, frequently paired in map questions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Sambhar Salt Lake (Rajasthan) is India's largest inland salt lake, covering ~230 sq km under normal conditions and expanding during monsoon. It is fed by seasonal streams draining the Aravallis and is of tectonic (fault-controlled) origin. It is a Ramsar site.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The phrasing 'drains into the Arabian Sea via the Rann of Kutch' is incorrect. Luni terminates in the Rann of Kutch — a seasonal saline marsh that floods during monsoon from both river inflow and tidal inflow. The Rann itself is a hydrologically closed or semi-closed basin; Luni does not flow through the Rann to the open Arabian Sea.

Value Addition:
• The Rann of Kutch floods annually during monsoon — creating a shallow saline lake ideal for flamingo breeding (Flamingo City).
• Sambhar Lake's salt has been harvested since antiquity — the Sambhar Salt Works are operated by Hindustan Salts Ltd.
• Luni's name means 'salty' in local dialect — reflecting its lower-course salinity.

solution.concept_anchor: Ganga right bank left bank tributaries correct identification

statement_analysis.statement: Gomti is a left-bank tributary of the Ganga, originating from Gomat Taal near Pilibhit in Uttar Pradesh.
statement_analysis.reason: Gomti is a Himalayan-origin left-bank tributary; it rises near Pilibhit (Gomat Taal) and joins the Ganga at Ghazipur.

statement_analysis.statement: Kosi, known as the 'Sorrow of Bihar', is a right-bank tributary of the Ganga.
statement_analysis.reason: Kosi is a LEFT-bank tributary of the Ganga — it originates in Nepal and joins the Ganga near Kursela, Bihar, from the north (left bank).

statement_analysis.statement: Betwa is a right-bank tributary of the Yamuna, which in turn is a right-bank tributary of the Ganga.
statement_analysis.reason: Betwa is a Peninsular river that joins the Yamuna on its right bank near Hamirpur (UP); Yamuna is itself a right-bank tributary of the Ganga at Prayagraj.

statement_analysis.statement: Ghaghra (Karnali) is a left-bank tributary of the Ganga that originates in Tibet.
statement_analysis.reason: Ghaghra (also called Karnali in its upper course in Nepal) originates in Tibet/Nepal and joins the Ganga near Chhapra in Bihar — a left-bank Himalayan tributary.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Wait — option b is the correct answer (only three correct). The strong distractor is option c (only two correct) — students who also doubt Statement 3's Betwa-Yamuna chain (thinking Betwa joins Ganga directly) will mark only two as correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Gomti as left-bank, Pilibhit origin — standard geography fact; mark Correct.
Statement 2: Kosi as 'right-bank' — Kosi joins from the north (LEFT bank); this is a classic left/right swap trap; mark Incorrect.
Statement 3: Betwa right-bank of Yamuna, Yamuna right-bank of Ganga — both levels correct; mark Correct.
Statement 4: Ghaghra/Karnali, Tibet origin, left-bank Ganga at Chhapra — mark Correct.
Three statements are correct — select option b (only three).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Kosi left/right bank trap is directly noted as a key_dimension trap. Bihar has both left-bank Himalayan tributaries (Kosi, Gandak, Ghaghra) and they all join from the north — the left bank when facing downstream. Students who associate Kosi with Bihar and Bihar with south of the Ganga may incorrectly assign it to the right bank. This is also reinforced by careless recall — 'Kosi floods Bihar from the north, so it must join from the south (right)' — which inverts the logic.
solution.final_explanation:
Left vs. right bank tributary identification for the Ganga is one of UPSC's most persistently tested map skills.

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Gomti — left bank, Pilibhit | Correct |
| Kosi — right-bank claim | Incorrect (it is left-bank) |
| Betwa (right of Yamuna) → Yamuna (right of Ganga) | Correct |
| Ghaghra/Karnali — left bank, Tibet origin | Correct |

Key rule: Left bank = northern tributaries from Nepal/Himalayas (Kosi, Gandak, Ghaghra, Gomti, Ramganga). Right bank = southern tributaries from Peninsula (Yamuna, Son, Ken, Betwa, Chambal).

Value Addition:
• Kosi has changed its course 120 km westward over the past 250 years — causing catastrophic flooding; hence 'Sorrow of Bihar'.
• Gandak (also called Narayani in Nepal) is another major left-bank Himalayan tributary joining near Hajipur-Sonepur.
• The famous Sonepur cattle fair (Asia's largest) occurs at the Gandak-Ganga confluence.

solution.concept_anchor: Brahmaputra flows westward Assam valley counter-intuitive direction
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion correct? — The Brahmaputra does indeed flow westward through the Assam valley (from Sadiya in the east to Dhubri in the west) — this is a documented and counter-intuitive geographic fact; Assertion is CORRECT.

Step 2: Is Reason correct? — The Brahmaputra valley is bounded to the north by the Himalayas and to the south by the Meghalaya Plateau and Purvanchal Hills — this correctly describes the topographic setting; Reason is CORRECT.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The Brahmaputra, after making its hairpin bend at Namcha Barwa, enters the longitudinal valley that runs east-west between these two highland blocks. The westward flow direction is determined by the tectonic valley orientation between the Himalayan and Meghalaya-Purvanchal topography. R does explain A — the valley's E-W orientation between these bounding highlands directs the river westward.
Both A and R are correct and R correctly explains A — select option a.
solution.final_explanation:
The Brahmaputra's westward flow through Assam contradicts the intuition that rivers in northeastern India flow east toward the Bay of Bengal.

Assertion Analysis: After the dramatic U-turn at Namcha Barwa (Arunachal-Tibet border), the Brahmaputra enters Assam at Sadiya and flows approximately 700 km westward before turning south near Dhubri to enter Bangladesh. This westward flow is a counter-intuitive but well-documented fact — CORRECT.

Reason Analysis: The Assam valley is a structural trough running E-W, flanked by the Eastern Himalayas and Arunachal to the north and the Meghalaya Plateau and Purvanchal Hills to the south. This E-W orientation is topographically accurate — CORRECT.

Causal Link: The valley's E-W tectonic orientation — between the Himalayan wall to the north and the southern highland rim — directs the river westward along the path of least resistance after its hairpin bend. R genuinely and causally explains A — the river flows west because the valley runs west.

Value Addition:
• The Brahmaputra carries the highest sediment load among Indian rivers — contributing to Majuli island formation and destruction.
• Assam's flood cycle is the most severe in India — the Brahmaputra's westward flow concentrates flood energy in the entire Assam plain.
• After Dhubri, the river enters Bangladesh as the Jamuna — it then joins the Ganga (Padma) and Meghna before reaching the Bay of Bengal.

solution.concept_anchor: Malwa Plateau Chambal Betwa lava capped black soil
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Chhota Nagpur Plateau) is a strong distractor because it is also a central Indian plateau drained by major rivers, and students who recall 'Chambal is in MP/Rajasthan' may associate it with the mineral-rich Chhota Nagpur rather than the lava-capped Malwa.
elimination_logic: The blank describes a lava-capped plateau north of the Vindhyas drained by Chambal and Betwa with fertile black soil.
Chhota Nagpur is Archaean (not lava-capped) and drained by Damodar — eliminate option b.
Telangana Plateau is south of the Vindhyas — eliminate option d.
Malwa Plateau is north of Vindhyas, lava-capped, drained by Chambal and Betwa — select option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Malwa-Chhota Nagpur distinction is a geographic-swap trap. Both are central Indian plateaus; both are important economically and geographically. However, their rock types are opposite — Malwa is lava-capped (Deccan Trap extension) with fertile black soil (Vertisol), while Chhota Nagpur is ancient Archaean crystalline with mineral wealth. Students who recall one without the other's precise identity may swap them.
solution.final_explanation:
Central Indian plateau identification requires distinguishing rock type, drainage, and geographic position relative to the Vindhyas.

• Option (a) Telangana Plateau: South of the Vindhyas, drained by Godavari and Krishna — not Chambal/Betwa; wrong drainage.
• Option (b) Chhota Nagpur Plateau: Archaean Precambrian crystalline rocks, not lava-capped; drained by Damodar, not Chambal/Betwa; associated with coal and minerals, not black cotton soil.
• Option (c) Malwa Plateau: Correct — lava-capped extension of Deccan Trap, north of Vindhyas, drained by Chambal and Betwa (both Yamuna tributaries); fertile black soil (Vertisol) supports cotton cultivation.
• Option (d) Chhattisgarh Plain: The Mahanadi basin — rice-growing region; not lava-capped or associated with Chambal/Betwa.

Value Addition:
• Malwa Plateau is the opium-growing region of Rajasthan/MP — historically significant in colonial trade.
• The Chambal ravines on the Malwa-Rajasthan border formed the historical dacoity belt — now partly under the National Chambal Sanctuary.
• Black cotton soil (Vertisol) over lava also characterises the Maharashtra Plateau — same geological origin.

solution.concept_anchor: NRLP Peninsular component Mahanadi Godavari surplus basins

statement_analysis.statement: The Mahanadi and Godavari are both identified as surplus river basins in the Peninsular component of the National River Linking Project.
statement_analysis.reason: Both Mahanadi and Godavari have high discharge relative to their utilisation — the NRLP Peninsular component designates them as surplus basins from which water can be transferred southward.

statement_analysis.statement: The Ken-Betwa link project connects two rivers that ultimately drain into the Bay of Bengal.
statement_analysis.reason: Ken and Betwa are both tributaries of the Yamuna, which drains into the Ganga and then into the Bay of Bengal — this part is true — BUT the rivers themselves are Peninsular tributaries of the Yamuna, draining into the Ganga system (Bay of Bengal). However, the statement's scope (that they drain into Bay of Bengal) is technically correct through their Yamuna-Ganga connection. Re-evaluating: Ken → Yamuna → Ganga → Bay of Bengal; Betwa → Yamuna → Ganga → Bay of Bengal. Both ultimately drain to Bay of Bengal via Yamuna-Ganga — this statement is actually CORRECT.

statement_analysis.statement: The Peninsular river linking component is designed to transfer surplus water exclusively from north-flowing rivers toward the south, reversing the natural drainage direction.
statement_analysis.reason: The Peninsular component transfers water from surplus eastern basins (Mahanadi, Godavari) toward deficit southern basins (Krishna, Pennar, Kaveri) — the transfer is broadly south-to-south, not 'north-to-south reversing natural drainage'. The framing 'exclusively north-flowing rivers' and 'reversing natural drainage' is an over-extension.

elimination_logic: Statement 1: Mahanadi and Godavari as surplus basins in NRLP Peninsular component — textbook NRLP geography; mark Correct.
Statement 2: Ken and Betwa draining into Bay of Bengal — both join Yamuna → Ganga → Bay of Bengal; technically correct; mark Correct.

Statement 3: 'Exclusively north-flowing rivers' and 'reversing natural drainage' — this over-extends the NRLP concept; Mahanadi and Godavari already flow east/southeast; the transfer doesn't reverse 'natural drainage direction' in a strict sense; mark Incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct — select option a.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses the scope-extension technique — adding 'exclusively' and 'reversing natural drainage direction' to a broadly true statement about inter-basin transfer. The Peninsular component does move water from high-discharge basins toward deficit basins, but the characterisation of this as 'reversing natural drainage' and 'exclusively north-flowing rivers' is a deliberate over-extension that makes the statement false.
solution.final_explanation:
The NRLP's Peninsular component involves a chain of links from Mahanadi southward to Kaveri — a complex network of canals and storage systems.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Mahanadi (highest discharge among Peninsular rivers relative to its size) and Godavari (largest Peninsular river) are the two designated surplus basins; water is to be transferred from them to Krishna, Pennar, and Kaveri.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Ken and Betwa both flow through MP and Rajasthan, eventually joining the Yamuna (in UP), which joins the Ganga, which drains into the Bay of Bengal. Their ultimate outlet is the Bay of Bengal.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Peninsular component moves water from eastern (Mahanadi, Godavari) basins to southern deficit basins — not 'exclusively north-to-south flow reversal'. All the rivers involved already flow broadly eastward/southward; the interlinking redirects a portion of surplus eastward flow toward the south.

Value Addition:
• The NRLP was conceptualised under the National Water Development Agency (NWDA) — established 1982.
• Ken-Betwa link will generate approximately 103 MW of hydropower in addition to irrigation benefits.
• The Godavari-Krishna link, if built, would create the longest inter-basin transfer canal in peninsular India.

formatted_presentation.display_text:
Consider the following statements about the National River Linking Project (NRLP):
1. The Mahanadi and Godavari are both identified as surplus river basins in the Peninsular component of the NRLP.
2. The Ken-Betwa link project connects two rivers that ultimately drain into the Bay of Bengal.
3. The Peninsular river linking component is designed to transfer surplus water exclusively from north-flowing rivers toward the south, reversing the natural drainage direction.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

(a) 1 and 2 only
(b) 2 and 3 only
(c) 1 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3
